hints: Remember that not every d-block element counts, focus on what the ion must have in its d-orbitals after it forms a stable ion.
walkthrough:
Separate d-block from transition element**
Think of the d-block as the location in the Periodic Table. A transition element is stricter. You must look at the ions it forms, not just the atom. For example, $\text{Sc}$ and $\text{Zn}$ sit in the d-block but are not transition elements because $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ has $3d^0$ and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ has $3d^{10}$.

State the precise test**
The test is: does it make at least one stable ion where the d-subshell is partly filled, so $d^1$ to $d^9$? If yes, it is a transition element. That is why $\text{Mn}$, $\text{Cr}$ and $\text{Ru}$ all qualify.
Final answer: A transition element is an element that forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete / partially filled d-subshell.

hints: Recall what $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ are reduced to in dilute acid, and remember $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ and $\text{Sn}^{4+}$ are both colourless so only the transition metal colour matters.
walkthrough:
Identify the reduction products**
Both oxidising agents oxidise $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ to $\text{Sn}^{4+}$, so they are themselves reduced. In acid, $\text{MnO}_4^-$ with $\text{Mn(+VII)}$ is reduced to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ with $\text{Mn(+II)}$. $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ with $\text{Cr(+VI)}$ is reduced to $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ with $\text{Cr(+III)}$.

Link to observed colours**
$\text{MnO}_4^-$ is intensely purple and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ in dilute solution is very pale pink, almost colourless. $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ is orange and $\text{Cr}^{3+}(\text{aq})$ is green. Because excess $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ is added, reduction goes to completion, so you see the full change.

Final answer: Dilute acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$: purple to colourless / pale pink ($\text{Mn}^{2+}$ formed).
Dilute acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$: orange to green ($\text{Cr}^{3+}$ formed).

hints: Start from the two half-equations, $\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^-$ and $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and think how to cancel the electrons.
walkthrough:
Balance electrons**
Tin is oxidised: $\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^-$. Dichromate is reduced: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$. To cancel $6e^-$, you need three tin half-equations for every one dichromate half-equation.

Combine and check**
Adding gives $$3\text{Sn}^{2+} + \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 3\text{Sn}^{4+} + 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms and charge: $3 \times (+2) -2 +14 = +18$ on the left, $3 \times (+4) + 2 \times (+3) = +18$ on the right. O and H also balance.

hints: Think about counting bonds to the central $\text{Ru}^{2+}$ ion, not the number of ligands, and recall what type of bond a ligand forms using its lone pair.
walkthrough:
Define coordination number correctly**
Picture the $\text{Ru}^{2+}$ ion at the centre surrounded by ligands. Coordination number counts the number of coordinate bonds from ligand donor atoms directly to the metal ion. Here that number is six.

Name the bond type**
Each bond is a coordinate or dative covalent bond formed when a ligand donates a lone pair into a vacant orbital on the $\text{Ru}^{2+}$ ion. For monodentate ligands like $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{SO}_2$, six bonds means six ligands.
Final answer: Six coordinate (dative covalent) bonds / six lone pairs donated to the central $\text{Ru}^{2+}$ ion.

hints: Use coordination number six to work out how many $\text{NH}_3$ ligands must be present alongside one $\text{Cl}^-$ and one $\text{SO}_2$, then add up the charges.
walkthrough:
Count the ligands**
Coordination number is six. One site is taken by $\text{Cl}^-$ and one site by $\text{SO}_2$, both monodentate. That leaves $6 - 1 - 1 = 4$ sites, so there must be four $\text{NH}_3$ molecules.

Work out the charge**
Add charges inside the brackets: $\text{Ru}^{2+} + \text{Cl}^- + 4 \times (0 \text{ for } \text{NH}_3) + 0 \text{ for } \text{SO}_2 = +1$. So the ion is $[\text{Ru}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}(\text{SO}_2)]^+$.

hints: Sketch an octahedron around Ru with four $\text{NH}_3$ in a plane and decide where to place $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ to make them adjacent versus opposite.
Remember to use solid wedges, hashed wedges and straight lines to show 3D octahedral geometry, not a flat cross.
Check that the $\text{SO}_2$ ligand is drawn bonded through S, written as Ru-S, not Ru-O.
walkthrough:
Set up the octahedral framework**
Put $\text{Ru}$ in the centre. An octahedral complex has six positions: four around the equator and one above and one below. Draw with proper 3D conventions, for example solid wedge coming out, hashed wedge going back, and normal lines in the plane.

Place the six ligands with Ru-S linkage**
Add four $\text{NH}_3$ ligands, one $\text{Cl}$ and one $\text{SO}_2$. Crucially, show the $\text{SO}_2$ attached via sulfur, so label it as $\text{Ru-SO}_2$ or $\text{Ru-S}$, with the S atom directly bonded to Ru.

Create the cis and trans pair**
In one box put $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ next to each other at $90^{\circ}$, this is the cis isomer. In the other box put $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ opposite each other at $180^{\circ}$, this is the trans isomer. Keep the four $\text{NH}_3$ ligands filling the remaining four octahedral sites in each diagram.

Final answer: Octahedral complex with $\text{Ru}$ at centre, four $\text{NH}_3$, one $\text{Cl}$ and one S-bonded $\text{SO}_2$ (Ru-S bond).
Isomer 1 (cis): $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ at $90^{\circ}$, adjacent positions.
Isomer 2 (trans): $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ at $180^{\circ}$, opposite positions.
Both drawn with correct 3D wedge / hashed bonds for octahedral shape.

hints: Think of the name given to isomerism where the same ligands can be side by side or across from each other in an octahedral or square planar complex.
walkthrough:
Name the isomer type**
You have just drawn two structures with the same formula but different spatial arrangements of $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ around the octahedron, cis ($90^{\circ}$) and trans ($180^{\circ}$). This is cis-trans isomerism, also called geometrical isomerism.
Final answer: Cis-trans / geometrical isomerism

hints: Start by thinking what happens to the energies of the five d-orbitals when ligands approach the metal ion.
Consider what part of the electromagnetic spectrum has energy matching the gap between the split d-orbitals.
Link the movement of an electron between d-orbitals to why we see a colour rather than white light.
walkthrough:
Split the d-orbitals**
In the free $\text{Ru}^{2+}$ ion the five 3d or 4d orbitals have the same energy. When ligands donate lone pairs, the d-orbitals that point directly at ligands are repelled more and rise in energy. The set splits into two levels with an energy gap, $\Delta$, that lies in the visible region.

Absorb light to promote an electron**
White light shines on the complex. A photon whose energy exactly matches the gap is absorbed, and a d-electron is excited from the lower set to the higher set. This is a d-d transition. $\text{Ru}^{2+}$ has a partially filled d-subshell, so this is possible.

See the complementary colour**
The light that is not absorbed passes through or is reflected. What your eye detects is white light minus the absorbed colour, which is the complementary colour. Different ligands split the d-orbitals by different amounts, so different wavelengths are absorbed and different colours are seen.

Final answer: Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two sets of different energy.
Electrons absorb visible light to be promoted / excited to the higher energy d-orbitals (d-d transition).
The colour observed is the complementary colour to that absorbed.
